To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(i) learned object embeddings are a key ingredient for complex visual reasoning and that (ii) self-supervised learning is crucial in order for these object representations to learn to reason.

(1) the use of learned embeddings of object-centric representations enables neural models to perform complex visual reasoning tasks; (2) attention over learned embeddings enables the neural model to reason about objects and relations in an object-centric fashion; and (3) self-supervised dynamics prediction enables the neural model not to rely on hand-crafted features and thus to generalize to unseen tasks.

1) a single network with a self-supervised learning objective, self-attention over object representations and a simple object-centric architecture can achieve state-of-the-art results on a range of visual reasoning tasks, and that 2) these results cannot be attained with any of the individual components, suggesting that all three components must be present for the best performance to emerge.
